name: Japanese Early Paleolithic hoax (Fujimura finds)
hook: An amateur's finds took Japan's human past back 700,000 years, until a newspaper filmed him burying them.

location.region: Miyagi Prefecture and other parts of eastern Japan

claim: Stone tools from many sites in eastern Japan, nearly all found by amateur Shinichi Fujimura, were said to show people in Japan long before 30,000 years ago: first at Zazaragi (1981), later 500,000 to 700,000 years ago at Kamitakamori.

claimed_age.label: >30,000 rising to >700,000 years
claimed_age.basis: Tephra layers dated by TL, fission-track and paleomagnetism (calendar-year estimates, not radiocarbon). Kamitakamori layers were put at 500,000 to 700,000 years.

accepted_age.label: Planted c. 1976-2000; mostly Jomon-period tools
accepted_age.basis: Mostly Jomon surface finds, planted from at least 1976 until November 2000. Verification found plough and iron marks, adhering topsoil and Jomon-type traits.

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: People reached Japan by about 30,000 uncalibrated 14C BP (older in calendar years); older claims such as Serizawa's were not accepted.

key_proponents: Shinichi Fujimura (amateur; made nearly all finds)

unambiguous_signal.note: The 1981 Zazaragi pieces were well-made tools, but critics said older chunky lithics and small flakes at several sites looked like natural breakage, not human work.

documented_context.note: Excavated finds were reported in place in dated tephra layers, but much material was picked from road and field cuttings, and critics saw signs of disturbance.

multiple_dating_methods.note: TL, fission-track and radiocarbon dates existed but conflicted; proponents used some TL and fission-track ages and set aside the rest.

multiple_labs.note: TL ages (Ichikawa) and fission-track ages (Koshimizu) came from different specialists.

professional_recovery.note: Digs were run by trained archaeologists (a research club, a museum, local boards), but the amateur Fujimura made nearly all key finds.

peer_reviewed_report.note: Main reports were excavation reports and symposium volumes; no peer-reviewed full report by about 1986 was found. Critics said press coverage came before reports.

material_accessible.note: Oda and Keally examined the lithics at Tohoku Museum of History and visited Babadan A in 1986; Takeoka said access narrowed after his 1998 critique.

independent_teams.note: Several bodies reported finds, but all traced to one research circle; even later 'confirmations' outside Miyagi, like Tama New Town 471-B (1987), came from the same group.

proponent_stake.note: No unusual stake was documented at the time. Fujimura's motives remain unclear; his fame and local tourism interest grew later.

objections.text: Clearly Jomon items, such as a stone drill and cord-marked pottery, were assigned to Paleolithic layers at Zazaragi, so later material was getting into older layers.
objections.raised_by: Shizuo Oda and Charles T. Keally
objections.outcome_note: The mechanism was planting, not natural vertical displacement; JAA reviewers found the tools closely matched Tohoku Jomon stone tools.

objections.text: Chunky lithics and small flakes from the lower, older strata at several sites showed unpatterned breakage from mixed local raw materials, more like natural damage than human flaking.
objections.raised_by: Shizuo Oda and Charles T. Keally
objections.outcome_note: Held: never validated as ancient tools. But natural breakage was not the eventual explanation; proponents met the critique with fabricated finds elsewhere from 1987, later shown to be planted.

objections.text: Tools lay flat on layer surfaces with no flaking debris or refitting pieces, though the deposits showed disturbance; much came from road and field cuttings.
objections.raised_by: Shizuo Oda and Charles T. Keally
objections.outcome_note: Re-digs found tools pushed into slits and tamped down, with no natural imprint in the soil (JAA).

objections.text: Proponents picked TL and fission-track ages that fit, and ignored reversals and conflicting TL and radiocarbon dates.
objections.raised_by: Shizuo Oda and Charles T. Keally
objections.outcome_note: Moot for the tools, which were planted; the tephra ages themselves were not what decided the case.

objections.text: Fifteen years of large digs in South Kanto found nothing older than about 30,000 years, so why would the oldest sites cluster in volcanically unstable Miyagi?
objections.raised_by: Shizuo Oda and Charles T. Keally
objections.outcome_note: Once Fujimura's material was removed, no Early/Middle Paleolithic sites remained in Miyagi; a seeming answer, fabricated finds at Tama New Town 471-B (1987), was also planted.

status_note: Re-digs and tool checks found planted tools; the JAA ruled (2002-03) that no Fujimura find can serve as Early or Middle Paleolithic evidence. Whether people reached Japan before ~40,000 years ago is a separate open question.
what_settled_it: Mainichi Shimbun photos of Fujimura burying tools (Nov 2000), his confession to 42 sites (2001), and JAA and prefectural checks: re-digs found tools pushed into slits, and tools bore plough and iron marks and topsoil. The JAA ruled the finds unusable in 2002.

timeline.event: Okamura, Kamata and amateur Shinichi Fujimura found the Sekki Bunka Danwakai research group in Miyagi.
Fujimura is planting tools on excavations by this year at the latest.
Zazaragi finds are declared to prove an Early/Middle Paleolithic in Japan, ending a long dispute.
Oda and Keally publish a detailed critique of the Miyagi claims; it is largely ignored.
Fabricated tools appear at Tama New Town 471-B, Tokyo, in strata older than 30,000 years, seeming to answer the South Kanto gap.
Kajiwara privately tells Keally the Kamitakamori tools can't be told from Jomon tools, a remark first published in 2000; no one treats it as a warning.
Toshiki Takeoka publishes a critique of the 'Early Paleolithic' finds; he later said the group stopped showing him artifacts afterward.
The team announces Kamitakamori 'postholes' and 'caches'; some finds are said to be over 700,000 years old.
Mainichi Shimbun prints photos of Fujimura burying tools; he admits planting at two sites only.
Fujimura confesses to planting at 42 sites.
JAA interim report: 30 sites checked so far are likely faked; a Zazaragi re-dig shows its early finds were planted too.
JAA publishes its 625-page final report; Miyagi keeps 19 of 148 Fujimura-linked sites as Paleolithic, all Late Paleolithic -- no older site remains.

falsifier: Tools from a Fujimura-linked layer, recovered by an independent team from undisturbed dated sediment with natural imprints and no plough, iron or topsoil traces, would show part of the corpus was genuine. Fujimura-free sites do not bear on this record.

confidence_note: Core facts come from JAA, Miyagi and peer-reviewed sources read in full. Site counts vary by definition; the claim year (1981, not 1976) and feature codes are judgment calls.
corrections: Not 'dozens' of sites: Fujimura was linked to about 186 'sites' (Hudson 2005). He confessed to 42; Miyagi listed 148 involving him, keeping 19 as Paleolithic. The Agency for Cultural Affairs counted 55 sites, plus 3 more from records.
At first (Nov 2000) Fujimura admitted only two sites, and his institute called the Kamitakamori posthole rings genuine; the JAA later judged those features natural or faked.
The filming was on 22 Oct 2000 at Kamitakamori, after a Sept 2000 photo at Soshin-Fudozaka; the Mainichi story ran on 5 Nov 2000 (Keally 2000).
Some reviews date the faking to the 1980s (Nakazawa 2017); Hudson 2005 and the verification reports trace it to at least 1976.
The rejection was in two steps: a JAA interim verdict in May 2002, then the final report in May 2003.
notes: Warnings were in print before 2000: Oda & Keally (1986) and Takeoka (1998). Keally (2000) lists 1986 points never answered, such as tools always lying flat on layer surfaces and the lack of flaking debris. After 1986, chunky lithics stopped appearing and finer bifacial tools did (Keally 2000). Takeoka's often-cited red-flag list is post-exposure (Asahi, 10 Nov 2000), not from his 1998 paper. The finds reached school textbooks and Renfrew & Bahn's 2000 textbook (Hudson 2005; Oda 2014). In Jan 2001 Miyagi defended three sites as untamperable; all three were later rejected. Fujimura-free candidates for pre-40,000-year occupation (e.g., Kanedori) are a separate open question (Nakazawa 2017).

open_issues: Did not compute a precise IntCal20 calibration for the 30,000 BP orthodoxy limit; labelled it as uncalibrated 14C BP instead, since an exact conversion could not be verified with available tools and an unverified number risks fabrication.

Did not add the JAA special committee's 625-page 2003 final report as its own source entry; already cited via S7, and confirming full bibliographic details was out of scope for this revision's budget.
Did not add that Takeoka later served on the JAA's artifact-verification working group; tangential, dropped for length budget.
Did not add the breakdown of the 1,372 re-examined pieces (561 excavated / 659 section-face / 152 surface) or the Zazaragi tree-throw detail; dropped for length budget.
Did not change independent_methods_count (kept at 4); all dating lines (TL/fission-track/paleomagnetism) date the tephra, not the tools, and depend on one finder's in-place association.
Kept year_claimed at 1981 (first public claim of tools older than 30,000 years); no source found confirming an earlier report already made that claim, though planting dates to at least 1976 (S1).

D19 re-rating 2026-09-23: unchanged — refuted fits: hoax exposed (filmed planting, confession, JAA re-digs). Pre-40 ka Japan without Fujimura is a separate question and not part of this record's claim.
